Printer troubleshooting

Laser and inkjet printers

First identify the printer technology and where the problem occurs: making the image, moving the paper, or delivering the print job. Use a built-in test page to help separate the printer from the computer, application, and network.

Two printing methods

Powder versus liquid ink

LaserInkjet
Image materialFine toner powder.Liquid ink ejected through tiny nozzles.
How it reaches paperAn imaging drum forms the toner image; a transfer component moves it to the paper.The printhead deposits ink directly onto the paper.
Finishing the imageA fuser bonds toner using heat and pressure.Ink dries or is absorbed by the paper. An inkjet does not use a laser-style toner fuser.
Common maintenanceToner replacement, cleaning, calibration, and the model’s maintenance kit.Ink replacement, nozzle checks, head cleaning, alignment, and feeder cleaning.
Consumable layoutThe drum may be separate or built into the cartridge.The printhead may be built into a cartridge or remain inside the printer.
Laser printing

The seven stages

StageWhat happens
1 · ProcessingThe printer turns the received job into a page image.
2 · ChargingThe drum receives a uniform electrical charge.
3 · ExposingThe laser changes the charge in selected areas of the drum.
4 · DevelopingToner forms the image on the drum.
5 · TransferringThe toner image moves from the drum to paper, directly or through an intermediate transfer system.
6 · FusingHeat and pressure bond toner to the paper.
7 · CleaningResidual toner is removed from the drum so it can form the next image.

These stages repeat continuously during printing. Cleaning prepares the drum for the next cycle.

Print quality

Read the marks on the page

Toner rubs off

Check supported paper and the media setting first. They affect fusing. If those are correct and service tests show a fuser fault, service or replace the fuser as directed.

Faded laser print

Check toner level, toner-save mode, paper, and print-density settings. Low toner is one possible cause, not an automatic diagnosis.

Lines, spots, and repeated images

A damaged or dirty imaging surface can leave repeating defects. Measure their spacing and compare it with the model’s service guide. Drum, transfer, and fuser problems can produce different repeating marks; appearance alone may not identify the part.

Inkjet bands or missing colors

Check supply levels, then print a nozzle check. Missing segments suggest nozzles are not firing. Run the approved cleaning cycle and retest. Cleaning consumes ink; follow the maker’s limits rather than running it repeatedly without a result.

Alignment

Misaligned printed lines or doubled edges may call for alignment. Alignment does not refill a cartridge or clear a blocked nozzle.

Paper handling

Pickup, separation, and the paper path

Pickup roller

Grips the top sheet and starts it moving. If it turns but slips, inspect for dirt or worn rubber. Use the approved cleaning procedure before replacing a dirty roller.

Separation pad or roller

Holds back the remaining sheets so only one feeds. Multiple-sheet feeding can come from worn separation parts, damp or unsuitable paper, or an overloaded tray.

Feed and exit rollers

Move the sheet through and out of the printer. Inspect the actual jam location instead of replacing an unrelated roller.

Duplexer and ADF

A duplexer sends paper through a return path for two-sided printing. An automatic document feeder moves originals through a scanner. They have their own paper paths and can fail while ordinary printing still works.

Before replacing parts

Check paper size, type, condition, fill level, guides, and debris. Clear jams using the service procedure, then check for torn scraps. Let hot parts cool and disconnect power before service.

Jobs and connectivity

Find where printing stops

  • Built-in page fails: investigate the printer, supplies, paper, and hardware.
  • Built-in page works: continue with the computer, driver, connection, and queue.
  • Only one application fails: test another document and application.
  • Only one workstation fails: inspect its selected printer, local queue, driver, and port.
  • Everyone using a shared queue fails: check the shared host or print server as well as the printer.

Check for a paused queue, offline mode, and a blocked first job. Try normal cancellation first. If it fails, stop Print Spooler, clear the affected spool files, restart the service, and test again. Get authorization before discarding users’ jobs.

A successful ping alone does not prove printing works. Check the configured printer address, connection, and a real print job.

Other common faults

Settings and maintenance choices

Garbled output

Compare a built-in page with a computer-generated page. Check the correct model driver and supported print language, such as PCL or PostScript. Test another file before replacing hardware.

Wrong orientation or size

Check application page setup, driver settings, tray size, and scaling. These are configuration problems unless tests point elsewhere.

Unrecognized tray

Check that the tray is seated and that installed accessories are configured in the driver. Inspect the tray’s sensors or contacts when indicated.

Maintenance kits

Contents vary by model. A kit may include a fuser and several rollers, but do not assume every kit includes the failed part. Check the parts list and service interval.

Finish the repair

Repeat the original job and the relevant test page. Confirm feeding, print quality, and queued jobs are working, then record the repair and test result.
